title: A Survey on Swarming With Micro Air Vehicles: Fundamental Challenges and Constraints

subsections.section_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful starting point for MAV swarming is the networked multi-agent systems view, in which each vehicle is modeled as a node with local state, limited sensing, and neighbor-to-neighbor communication over a time-varying graph. In this abstraction, collective behavior is specified through distributed feedback laws that depend only on relative information and sparse message exchange, while convergence and robustness are characterized through graph-theoretic notions such as connectivity, Laplacian structure, and leader-follower interconnections ref [1], ref [35]. For MAVs, this viewpoint is especially relevant because payload, power, and onboard computation constraints make centralized estimation and control difficult to scale.

Within this framework, canonical coordination objectives provide the language for formulating swarm tasks. Consensus captures agreement on shared variables such as heading, velocity, or altitude offsets ref [1]; flocking augments agreement with velocity matching, cohesion, and collision avoidance ref [2]; formation control prescribes geometric patterns, often encoded through relative positions or complex-Laplacian constructions ref [11]. More asymmetric tasks arise in containment, where followers converge to the convex region spanned by multiple leaders ref [8], and in leader-follower tracking, where the swarm must estimate and follow a moving reference under uncertainty and noisy measurements ref [9]. These objectives are not disjoint; practical MAV missions often combine them, for example maintaining a formation while tracking a leader and preserving inter-agent separation.

The resulting problem formulation for MAV swarms is therefore a constrained distributed control problem: design local control and estimation laws so that the swarm achieves a prescribed collective objective despite bounded inputs, intermittent communication, and evolving interaction topology. Connectivity preservation is a first-order requirement because loss of graph links can invalidate the assumptions underlying consensus and formation guarantees; bounded distributed strategies explicitly address this issue ref [29]. More generally, cooperative regulation and transient synchronization perspectives connect swarm objectives to output regulation and disturbance rejection for agents with nontrivial dynamics ref [57]. This systems-level foundation motivates the remainder of the section, which specializes these abstract models to MAV-specific sensing, actuation, and safety constraints.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A convenient problem formulation for MAV swarms models each vehicle as a constrained dynamical agent coupled over a time-varying communication graph, with coordination objectives expressed at the state, output, or relative-position level. Within this view, consensus, synchronization, and output regulation become canonical primitives for distributed aerial cooperation, because they abstract altitude, velocity, heading, and task-variable agreement under limited local information. General distributed cooperative control formulations emphasize that the controller design must simultaneously account for graph topology, agent dynamics, and decentralized information patterns rather than treating coordination as a purely kinematic problem ref [10], ref [41].

For MAVs, these objectives are further shaped by hard actuator saturation, asynchronous updates, packet sparsity, and disturbance sensitivity. Predictive and event-triggered designs provide a natural mathematical framework for such settings by embedding communication and control decisions into constrained optimization, thereby reducing unnecessary transmissions while preserving coordinated behavior under asynchronous operation ref [10], ref [12]. The same constrained viewpoint is essential for maintaining inter-agent connectivity and collision-safe interaction neighborhoods, especially when bounded inputs and nonholonomic motion restrict feasible maneuvers ref [34].

Beyond unconstrained agreement, MAV swarm tasks often require richer leader-follower objectives, including containment inside a moving convex hull, formation tracking around a leader, and cooperative rejection of wind or modeling errors. Adaptive containment formulations address heterogeneous followers and uncertain leader dynamics ref [13], while distributed adaptive formation control captures shape maintenance with a moving reference ref [27]. More broadly, anti-disturbance cooperative control highlights robustness as a first-class design objective in networked systems ref [38]. Taken together, these models define MAV swarming as a distributed control problem over constrained, disturbed, and intermittently connected multi-agent systems rather than as idealized flocking alone ref [10], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central layer in MAV swarm problem formulation is the specification of coordination objectives beyond basic agreement, notably leader–follower consensus, formation tracking, and containment. In consensus-type tasks, each vehicle asymptotically aligns selected outputs or states with neighbors or designated leaders despite heterogeneity and time-varying interaction graphs. This perspective is particularly relevant for MAV teams with mismatched dynamics or sensing suites, where output-based adaptive consensus under switching directed topologies provides a natural abstraction for distributed coordination under intermittent communication ref [21]. Related leader-following formulations for heterogeneous second-order nonlinear agents further capture the practical case in which a subset of MAVs tracks a virtual command trajectory while preserving distributed implementation under directed switching graphs ref [29].

Formation objectives refine consensus by imposing geometric constraints on relative positions or velocities. For MAV swarms, time-varying formation tracking is especially important because the desired shape often deforms during obstacle avoidance, surveillance, or target encirclement. Distributed designs for second-order agents explicitly characterize how tracking and shape maintenance can be achieved simultaneously ref [10], while adaptive time-varying formation results for higher-order linear dynamics show how the same objective can be generalized to agents with richer internal models and uncertain couplings ref [40]. Event-triggered formation stabilization and tracking additionally introduce a resource-aware problem formulation in which control updates are generated only when needed, reflecting bandwidth and onboard computation limits typical of MAV platforms ref [52].

Containment control provides another foundational objective when the swarm is partitioned into leaders and followers and the goal is to drive followers into the convex hull spanned by leaders. This formulation is useful for corridor guidance, perimeter shaping, and safe motion within moving supervisory boundaries. Classical distributed containment results for linear multi-agent systems formalize the graph-theoretic conditions under which this objective is feasible ref [27], while necessary and sufficient conditions without velocity measurement better match sensing-limited MAV settings where full state feedback is unavailable ref [33]. Extensions to fractional-order uncertain systems further emphasize that containment formulations remain meaningful even under nonideal dynamics and modeling uncertainty ref [11]. Collectively, these objective classes define the mathematical backbone for MAV swarming: distributed control laws must achieve agreement, shape regulation, or enclosure under switching topologies, partial measurements, and heterogeneous agent dynamics.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central coordination objective in MAV swarms is containment, where follower vehicles are driven into the convex hull spanned by one or more leaders rather than to a single rendezvous point. This formulation is especially relevant to surveillance, convoy protection, and cooperative exploration, because it naturally accommodates moving references, subgroup guidance, and heterogeneous roles. In the literature, containment has been posed for heterogeneous and even singular agent models, highlighting that the problem extends beyond idealized identical-integrator abstractions and must account for mismatched internal dynamics across agents ref [25], ref [18].

For MAV swarms, the problem formulation becomes more realistic when communication and timing are imperfect. Discrete-time asynchronous updates with time-varying delays alter the effective neighbor information available to each vehicle and can significantly affect convergence and stability margins, making them a natural model for onboard wireless coordination ref [31]. Directed interaction graphs and event-based broadcasting further reflect practical bandwidth limitations, since MAVs often cannot maintain continuous all-to-all exchange; containment laws under directed topologies therefore provide an important bridge between graph-theoretic formulations and implementable swarm protocols ref [13].

Another key issue is that aerial vehicles operate under strict actuation and safety limits. Containment designs that explicitly account for velocity and acceleration saturations are therefore more representative of MAV operation than unconstrained controllers ref [12]. The same applies to nonlinear uncertain dynamics, dynamic leaders, and partial loss of actuation authority: adaptive or command-filter-based containment formulations have been developed to address bounded unknown nonlinearities, actuator failures, and moving leader sets ref [21], ref [25]. Collectively, these models motivate a constrained distributed control problem in which each MAV must achieve set-based coordination using local, delayed, and event-driven information while respecting nonlinear flight-envelope limitations ref [12], ref [18], ref [21], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of MAV Swarming: System Models, Coordination Objectives, and Problem Formulation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A useful final layer in the problem formulation of MAV swarming is the treatment of higher-level collective objectives beyond basic agreement, namely containment, formation tracking, and persistent cooperative motion. In containment, a subset of followers is driven into the convex hull spanned by virtual or physical leaders, which is particularly relevant for perimeter guidance, safe corridor navigation, and human-supervised swarm steering. The general consensus perspective clarifies that containment can be interpreted as a leader–follower extension of agreement dynamics under directed interaction graphs ref [39]. For MAVs, however, this objective must be posed under heterogeneous vehicle dynamics, limited measurements, and nonideal communication rather than as an abstract kinematic task.

The literature therefore formulates containment and formation objectives with increasingly realistic constraints. Representative models include general linear follower dynamics with explicit communication delays ref [24], high-order agents with heterogeneous delays ref [29], and second-order nonlinear agents under intermittent communications ref [40]. Formation tracking further extends the objective from convergence to a static geometric pattern toward maintaining a moving reference shape around one or more leaders, often via observer-based architectures when full state exchange is unavailable ref [33]. Closely related persistent formation formulations emphasize simultaneous generation and stabilization of a desired shape over time, making them natural abstractions for cooperative sensing and area coverage by MAV teams ref [50].

These formulations also motivate predictive and resource-aware control problem statements. Hybrid distributed MPC has been used to couple containment with distributed sensing objectives, highlighting the dual role of swarm geometry in both control and information gathering ref [16]. Likewise, self-triggered distributed MPC for flocking explicitly incorporates communication/update sparsity into the optimization loop, which is highly aligned with onboard computation and bandwidth limits in MAV swarms ref [18]. Taken together, this body of work suggests that MAV swarm problem formulations should jointly specify graph structure, agent dynamics, collective objective, and operational constraints such as delays, intermittent links, and sensing-task coupling, since these factors fundamentally shape the feasibility of distributed coordination ref [16], ref [18], ref [24], ref [29], ref [33], ref [40], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A foundational class of distributed coordination strategies for MAV swarms is consensus-based control, where each vehicle updates its state from locally exchanged neighbor information rather than centralized commands. This paradigm provides the basic machinery for agreement on position, velocity, heading, or auxiliary coordination variables under sparse communication graphs, and remains attractive for MAVs because of its scalability and limited global-information requirements. Early unifying treatments established how graph topology, Laplacian structure, and directed interactions determine convergence and robustness properties of coordinated networked systems ref [1], while broader cooperative-control formulations connected these ideas to practical distributed stabilization and task allocation problems in multi-agent settings ref [35].

For dynamic swarm motion, consensus laws are often extended to flocking, where alignment must be achieved together with collision avoidance and spatial cohesion. The flocking framework in ref [2] is especially influential because it formalizes how local interaction rules generate coherent group motion, a core requirement for MAV teams operating in cluttered or GPS-denied environments. Beyond first-order agreement, MAVs frequently require second- or higher-order models to capture translational dynamics; accordingly, distributed gain design for nonlinear second-order agents ref [12] and consensus protocols for higher-order dynamics under switching directed topologies ref [45] are important steps toward realistic aerial-swarm implementations.

Consensus mechanisms also underpin distributed formation maintenance. Complex-Laplacian formulations enable shape control with compact encoding of planar formations and are relevant when MAV swarms must preserve geometric patterns using only relative information ref [11]. In practice, however, pure agreement is insufficient unless inter-vehicle communication links remain intact; bounded distributed controllers that explicitly preserve connectivity therefore address a major MAV constraint, namely the fragility of ad hoc wireless interaction graphs during maneuvering ref [29]. More generally, distributed output-regulation and transient-synchronization ideas extend consensus from state agreement to coordinated tracking of exogenous signals, offering a bridge from basic synchronization to task-oriented swarm behavior ref [57].

Overall, classical consensus and flocking methods form the conceptual backbone of distributed MAV coordination, but their practical use depends on accommodating nonlinear dynamics, switching graphs, formation geometry, and connectivity preservation within computationally lightweight local controllers ref [1], ref [2], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A second major line of distributed coordination for MAV swarms extends basic consensus laws with predictive, event-triggered, adaptive, and observer-based mechanisms to better cope with limited communication, actuation bounds, and model uncertainty. In this literature, model predictive control (MPC) is especially attractive because it embeds input and state constraints directly into the coordination law. Distributed MPC formulations have been used to guarantee consensus under actuator saturation and related admissibility constraints, making them relevant for thrust- and velocity-limited MAV platforms ref [43]. Closely related work combines predictive control with event triggering to support asynchronous coordination, thereby reducing unnecessary transmissions while preserving distributed decision making under nonuniform update times ref [10].

Event-triggered designs also appear outside the predictive setting. For heterogeneous discrete-time agents, distributed event-triggered controllers have been developed to maintain consensus with fewer communication updates, which is valuable for resource-constrained onboard radios and processors ref [45]. At the same time, adaptive disturbance-rejection strategies on directed graphs address unknown exogenous inputs and modeling errors without requiring centralized disturbance estimation, improving robustness in the presence of wind and inter-vehicle mismatches ref [18]. For output regulation objectives, dynamic-compensator-based distributed schemes offer a systematic way to synchronize agent outputs to shared references or exosystems using only local interaction information ref [41].

A further trend is to incorporate learning and state reconstruction into distributed coordination. Distributed learning consensus has been studied for heterogeneous high-order nonlinear systems with output constraints, highlighting how coordination can be maintained even when measurable outputs are limited or constrained ref [44]. Neural-network-based cooperative learning controllers similarly target nonlinear discrete-time agents and compensate uncertain dynamics in a consensus framework ref [16]. For nonlinear output-consensus tracking, observer-based and command-filtered backstepping designs provide a practical architecture to estimate unmeasured states while avoiding the complexity explosion of recursive nonlinear control laws ref [45]. Taken together, these methods broaden the design space for MAV swarms beyond classical consensus, particularly when distributed implementation must tolerate constraints, asynchronous communication, and uncertain dynamics.

subsections.section_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A prominent direction for distributed MAV swarm coordination is event-triggered and self-triggered control, which reduces continuous communication and control updates while preserving collective objectives such as consensus and formation maintenance. In contrast to periodic schemes, these methods update only when local triggering conditions are violated, making them attractive for bandwidth- and energy-limited aerial platforms. Foundational distributed event-triggered protocols establish consensus using locally available neighbor information and explicitly address the exclusion of pathological fast triggering behaviors, thereby improving practical implementability in networked multi-agent settings ref [45], ref [24], ref [49].

Several extensions refine this idea for more realistic swarm scenarios. Distributed event-triggered estimators enable both leaderless and leader-following consensus when agents cannot access neighbors’ states continuously, replacing persistent communication with estimator-based reconstruction from intermittent transmissions ref [43]. State-dependent triggering thresholds further adapt update frequency to the current coordination error, offering a more flexible tradeoff between convergence performance and communication load for general linear agent models ref [48]. For coordination tasks beyond pure agreement, event-triggered mechanisms have also been developed for distributed formation stabilization and trajectory tracking, which is particularly relevant to MAV swarms executing geometric patterns or cooperative motion under limited inter-agent exchange ref [52].

Event-triggered ideas also integrate naturally with optimization and prediction. Distributed model predictive control has been used to enforce consensus for nonlinear second-order agents while accounting for future state evolution, a useful feature when swarm motion constraints and transient behavior matter ref [32]. At the same time, event-triggered adaptive dynamic programming introduces an approximate optimal control perspective for nonlinear coordination, reducing update burden while improving cost-aware distributed decision making ref [26]. Taken together, these works suggest that event-driven coordination is not merely a communication-saving add-on, but a broader design paradigm for scalable MAV swarms operating under tight onboard computation, sensing, and networking constraints ref [24], ref [26], ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Event-triggered and self-regulated communication strategies are particularly attractive for MAV swarms because they reduce continuous broadcasting and control updates, thereby saving bandwidth, computation, and onboard energy while retaining distributed implementability. In this line, distributed event-triggered consensus laws replace periodic communication with state-dependent triggering conditions, so agents exchange information only when local errors exceed prescribed thresholds ref [58]. This basic idea has been extended to leader-following settings through dynamic triggering mechanisms that introduce internal variables to avoid overly conservative update rules and to improve convergence under linear agent models ref [17].

A major trend is the integration of event-triggering with adaptive and predictive control. Distributed adaptive event-triggered schemes compensate for parametric uncertainty or unknown couplings while still guaranteeing consensus with sparse communication ref [35], and related adaptive leader-following designs further emphasize fully distributed gain adaptation without centralized topology information ref [49]. In parallel, adaptive event-triggered distributed model predictive control combines finite-horizon optimization with communication scheduling, offering a systematic way to respect state and input constraints while reducing unnecessary transmissions ref [24]. For MAV swarms operating close to actuation and safety limits, this predictive-event-triggered combination is especially relevant.

Beyond consensus, event-triggered coordination has also been specialized to richer collective behaviors and more realistic operating conditions. Asynchronous distributed event-triggered circle formation illustrates how agents can coordinate geometric patterns despite non-simultaneous updates, a useful property for heterogeneous MAV platforms with unsynchronized clocks or variable processing rates ref [51]. Hybrid event-triggered mechanisms have also been proposed for stochastic tracking problems, where triggering logic must account for noise and random disturbances rather than ideal deterministic measurements ref [57]. Overall, these works suggest that event-triggered distributed control is not merely a communication-saving add-on, but a flexible coordination paradigm for scalable MAV swarms under limited global knowledge and intermittent information exchange ref [58], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Distributed Control and Coordination Strategies for MAV Swarms - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final class of distributed coordination methods particularly relevant to MAV swarms focuses on reducing communication and computation through event-triggered, self-triggered, and observer-assisted designs. Relative to continuous exchange, these schemes update control actions only when local conditions indicate loss of coordination accuracy, thereby better matching bandwidth- and energy-constrained aerial platforms. The broader rationale follows the consensus literature, which established how distributed agreement can be achieved under sparse graph information and imperfect connectivity assumptions, providing the conceptual baseline for such resource-aware extensions ref [39].

Event-triggered strategies have been developed for heterogeneous multi-agent systems under both fixed and switching topologies, showing that consensus can be maintained despite dynamic interaction graphs while avoiding unnecessary transmissions ref [27]. Closely related leader-tracking formulations trigger updates from local state errors rather than periodic schedules, enabling distributed tracking of an active leader with reduced communication load ref [48]. Self-triggered formulations push this idea further by predicting the next required update instant in advance; in particular, distributed model predictive flocking schemes combine local optimization with self-triggering to preserve collective motion while lowering sampling and coordination frequency ref [18].

Observer-based designs are also important when MAVs lack full-state measurements or must estimate neighbors and leader states from partial information. Observer-based formation tracking in leader-follower settings supports distributed shape maintenance with limited sensing ref [33], while observer-based consensus for nonlinear systems with interval control inputs addresses bounded actuation and partial-state feedback, both highly relevant to small aerial vehicles ref [45]. Beyond estimation and triggering, adaptive and learning-enhanced methods seek resilience to uncertainty and disturbances. Reinforcement-learning-based resilient adaptive optimal control illustrates how distributed agents can improve performance online under uncertain environments, although its practical deployment in MAV swarms remains constrained by onboard computation and safety-certification demands ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first and pervasive constraint in MAV swarms is that coordination laws are rarely executed under continuous, delay-free, and globally available information. Classical consensus theory shows that stability and convergence fundamentally depend on the interaction graph, the timing of updates, and the information locally exchanged among agents, making communication structure itself a control design variable rather than a mere implementation detail ref [1]. For MAVs, this implies that limited bandwidth, processor load, and intermittent links directly shape achievable swarm behaviors, especially for agreement, synchronization, and leader–follower coordination.

To reduce channel occupancy, event-triggered and sampled-data strategies replace periodic broadcasts with state-dependent transmissions, but this introduces nonuniform update times, asynchronous information sets, and more intricate stability conditions. Distributed event-triggered formulations demonstrate that consensus can be preserved while significantly lowering communication demand, provided triggering rules are designed to exclude pathological fast transmissions and to account for local estimation errors ref [66], ref [6], ref [52]. Complementarily, sampled-data cooperative control highlights that discrete sensing and actuation inherently induce approximation and delay effects, which become more pronounced in fast MAV maneuvers and under switching interaction topologies ref [15].

Information constraints are further compounded by sensing noise, bounded control authority, and the need to preserve network connectivity. Noisy relative measurements degrade tracking accuracy in leader–follower architectures and generally require robustness margins in distributed estimators and controllers ref [9]. Likewise, bounded connectivity-preserving strategies show that maintaining a viable communication graph may conflict with aggressive motion objectives, especially when vehicles must respect actuation limits ref [29]. In discrete-time settings, consensus under velocity constraints, delays, and nonconvex admissible sets underscores how communication imperfections and motion constraints are tightly coupled in practical swarm deployment ref [49].

Overall, the literature suggests that MAV swarm algorithms should be communication-aware by design: sparse and event-based exchange can improve scalability, but only when paired with robustness to delays, noise, switching graphs, and bounded inputs. This trade-off between information economy and closed-loop guarantees is central to any realistic distributed architecture for micro aerial swarms ref [1], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central response to communication scarcity in MAV swarms is event-triggered and aperiodic coordination, where information is exchanged only when local error measures exceed prescribed thresholds rather than at fixed rates. This design directly targets bandwidth and energy limits while preserving distributed operation under intermittent updates. Recent work has extended this idea to asynchronous predictive coordination, showing that agents can optimize over future motion while communicating at nonuniform instants, thereby reducing channel occupancy without reverting to centralized scheduling ref [43]. Related aperiodic MPC formulations similarly demonstrate that consensus-oriented coordination can be maintained when update times are irregular and locally determined, an assumption that is often closer to practical embedded MAV implementations than synchronous periodic control ref [49].

The literature also makes clear that reduced communication comes at the cost of more delicate stability analysis, especially for heterogeneous, switching, or directed interaction graphs. Event-triggered controllers have been developed for discrete-time heterogeneous systems, for leader-following under switching networks, and for general linear agents on directed graphs with fully continuous communication-free triggering logics ref [73], ref [15], ref [52]. These results are relevant to MAV swarms because they show how consensus guarantees can be retained despite asynchronous sampling, topology variation, and unequal onboard dynamics, but typically only under carefully designed triggering rules that exclude pathological behaviors and preserve graph-level connectivity assumptions.

Beyond pure consensus, information constraints interact with uncertainty, delay, and limited observability. Stochastic leader-following with input delay has been addressed through event-triggered mean-square consensus conditions, highlighting that packet irregularity and actuation lag must be analyzed jointly rather than as separable effects ref [19]. For nonlinear cooperative regulation, distributed event-triggered designs show that communication-aware updates can still support robust output regulation objectives ref [28]. At the sensing layer, discontinuous observations further complicate distributed consensus because each MAV reasons over state estimates derived from imperfect local measurements rather than smooth shared trajectories ref [30]. Collectively, these studies suggest that communication-aware swarm algorithms should be co-designed with estimator structure, delay tolerance, and task-level regulation objectives rather than appended as a secondary networking layer.

subsections.section_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central response to communication scarcity in MAV swarms is to replace periodic broadcasting with event-driven information exchange. Distributed event-triggered and self-triggered controllers reduce channel occupancy by transmitting only when local state errors or predicted deviations exceed prescribed thresholds, thereby preserving consensus or coordination performance with fewer updates ref [79], ref [45], ref [49]. For MAV platforms, this design choice is especially attractive because it directly addresses limited bandwidth, contention in shared wireless media, and onboard energy constraints, but it also shifts algorithm design toward trigger synthesis, exclusion of pathological fast triggering, and robustness to irregular inter-update intervals ref [79], ref [43], ref [45].

Irregular communication interacts strongly with asynchronous operation and delay. Delay-dependent consensus analysis for second-order agents shows that stability margins depend explicitly on communication latency, implying that aggressive sparsification of transmissions cannot be separated from the closed-loop dynamics ref [53]. Related asynchronous containment results for heterogeneous agents further indicate that agents can still coordinate under non-simultaneous updates, but convergence conditions become tied to update schedules and heterogeneity across followers and leaders ref [50]. In MAV swarms, where clocks, processors, and links are naturally unsynchronized, these results motivate controllers that are delay-aware rather than merely communication-efficient ref [53], ref [50].

Beyond low-level consensus, recent work embeds communication constraints into higher-level coordination objectives. Distributed output-regulation formulations account for constrained information exchange in heterogeneous networks, clarifying how limited neighbor information affects tracking and disturbance rejection capabilities ref [25]. Likewise, communication-aware motion planning integrates temporal and spatial logic specifications with explicit communication considerations, demonstrating that information availability must be treated as a planning resource rather than an afterthought ref [24]. Event-triggered estimators further extend this idea by allowing leaderless and leader-following consensus with reduced direct communication through local state reconstruction ref [43]. Collectively, these studies point toward MAV swarm architectures in which communication policies, estimators, and task planners are co-designed under bounded information flow ref [24], ref [25], ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central response to communication scarcity in MAV swarms is to replace periodic exchange with event-triggered or sampled-data coordination, thereby transmitting only when local state discrepancies become significant. In consensus and containment settings, distributed event-triggered laws substantially reduce channel usage while preserving convergence under directed graphs and decentralized triggering conditions, which is particularly relevant for bandwidth-limited aerial teams operating over shared wireless links ref [80], ref [13], ref [35], ref [36]. For MAV deployment, the key implication is that communication policies become part of the control design itself: stability margins, inter-event times, and robustness to stale neighbor information must be co-designed rather than treated as networking afterthoughts ref [80], ref [35], ref [36].

These benefits are tempered by the fact that MAV swarms rarely operate synchronously. Asynchronous updates, nonuniform sampling, and time-varying delays distort the effective interaction topology seen by each vehicle, especially in fast maneuvers or occluded environments. Results on asynchronous containment for discrete-time second-order systems and asynchronous event-triggered circle formation show that coordination can still be maintained without global clocks, but the admissible delay and triggering conditions become more restrictive, and transient performance typically deteriorates as information ages ref [82], ref [51]. Similarly, sampled-data observer designs for leader-follower tracking highlight that bounded performance can be retained with intermittent measurements, provided estimation and control are explicitly matched to the update process ref [44].

Packet loss further exposes the fragility of distributed aerial coordination because dropped packets simultaneously reduce observability and break the assumptions of nominal graph connectivity. This issue is especially concrete in quadcopter leader-follower experiments, where distributed cooperative control under packet dropouts must absorb missing neighbor data without destabilizing the formation ref [40]. Taken together, these works suggest that communication-aware MAV swarm algorithms should be evaluated not only by nominal convergence, but by their tolerance to irregular broadcasts, delayed containment information, lossy links, and observer mismatch under directed interaction graphs ref [82], ref [13], ref [40], ref [44].

subsections.section_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms
subsections.subsection_title: Communication, Sensing, and Information Constraints in MAV Swarms - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final dimension of information constraint in MAV swarms is the deliberate reduction of communication through sampled-data, event-triggered, and self-triggered coordination. These strategies are attractive for resource-limited aerial platforms because they lower channel occupancy and onboard processing, but they also replace continuous feedback with sporadic state updates and stale neighbor information. Sampled-data consensus results show that stability can still be preserved under missing control inputs, provided the update law explicitly accounts for the resulting hold behavior and inter-sample evolution ref [20]. Likewise, event-triggered consensus and containment schemes for heterogeneous or discrete-time multi-agent systems reduce unnecessary transmissions, but they make convergence dependent on trigger design, topology persistence, and robustness to asynchronous executions ref [27], ref [34].

For motion-level coordination, self-triggered and hybrid MPC formulations provide a principled way to couple communication scheduling with prediction-based control. In flocking, self-triggered distributed MPC trades communication frequency against prediction horizon and constraint satisfaction, illustrating how sparse updates can retain coherent collective motion at the cost of more conservative designs ref [18]. Hybrid MPC for containment and distributed sensing further shows that sensing objectives and communication decisions cannot be separated cleanly: limited information flow directly shapes feasible leader-follower geometry and coverage performance ref [16]. More generally, intermittent communication in nonlinear second-order containment problems confirms that practical guarantees often weaken from continuous-tracking notions to boundedness or ultimate convergence under explicit communication assumptions ref [40].

These works highlight that communication-aware swarm design is not only a control problem but also an algorithmic one. Studies of differently coupled collective systems emphasize that the admissible swarm behaviors depend on what information can be sensed, exchanged, and acted upon locally ref [36]. Related evidence from modular robotic collectives shows that communication capacity can fundamentally alter achievable group motion patterns, a lesson that transfers directly to MAV swarms operating under bandwidth-limited radios ref [54]. Consequently, scalable aerial swarms increasingly require co-design of triggers, prediction, topology management, and task objectives, rather than treating communication as a transparent substrate ref [16], ref [27], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first safety-critical challenge in MAV swarms is the presence of hard physical limits on thrust, attitude rate, and velocity, which invalidate unconstrained consensus or formation controllers. Several distributed designs explicitly incorporate bounded inputs and state restrictions rather than treating them as secondary implementation issues. Constrained optimal consensus formulations account for admissible operating regions during coordination ref [24], while bounded distributed controllers have been used to preserve connectivity without demanding unachievable control effort ref [29]. For nonlinear agents, adaptive consensus-tracking schemes with explicit state constraints further show how safety envelopes can be enforced during transient evolution ref [42]. In discrete-time settings, velocity-constrained consensus has also been studied under nonconvex constraints, delays, and switching topologies, highlighting the relevance of kinematic bounds to realistic networked flight ref [49].

Within swarm flight, these constraints couple directly to collision risk. Distributed MPC is particularly attractive because collision avoidance, obstacle avoidance, and formation objectives can be handled in one receding-horizon optimization with explicit constraints ref [30]. However, online optimization alone does not remove the difficulty created by actuator saturation; if saturations are ignored, aggressive avoidance or reconfiguration maneuvers may become infeasible. This motivates consensus and coordination laws that are saturation-aware by design, including fully distributed semiglobal consensus under input saturation ref [32] and event-triggered global consensus schemes that explicitly account for saturation effects ref [56].

Constraint handling is also intertwined with robustness. In MAV swarms, uncertainty, aerodynamic disturbances, and component degradation can drive agents toward the boundary of safe operating sets, so constraint-aware control must often be paired with adaptation or fault accommodation. Distributed adaptive fault-tolerant control addresses this by maintaining coordinated behavior despite uncertain dynamics and failures ref [47]. Overall, the literature suggests that for MAV swarms, safety cannot be layered on top of nominal coordination; instead, bounded actuation, constrained motion, collision avoidance, and fault tolerance must be co-designed at the distributed control level ref [24], ref [30], ref [42], ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central safety-critical issue in MAV swarms is the mismatch between coordination laws designed at the kinematic level and the tight actuator limits of real platforms. Input saturation can destroy consensus or formation guarantees, induce sluggish transients, and amplify inter-vehicle spacing errors during aggressive maneuvers. To address this, constrained distributed control has been explicitly incorporated into consensus design through model predictive control, which handles admissible input sets directly, and through nonlinear command-filtered backstepping methods that compensate for saturation while avoiding repeated differentiation in tracking controllers ref [45], ref [9]. Event-triggered disturbance-observer schemes further combine communication efficiency with explicit treatment of bounded inputs, which is especially relevant for battery-limited MAV networks ref [51].

Beyond nominal saturation, swarm operation must remain reliable under disturbances, modeling uncertainty, and partial loss of actuation. Adaptive disturbance-rejection strategies on directed graphs improve robustness against unknown exogenous inputs, while the broader anti-disturbance literature emphasizes distributed estimation and compensation mechanisms suitable for cooperative aerial systems exposed to wind and wake effects ref [18], ref [38]. In parallel, fault-tolerant consensus and formation controllers have been developed for actuator degradation and failures, including neural-network-based adaptive schemes for uncertain nonlinear agents and distributed laws that accommodate time-varying actuator faults or outright actuator failures during formation evolution ref [14], ref [37], ref [43].

Taken together, these works suggest that safe MAV swarming requires an integrated treatment of hard input bounds, uncertainty rejection, and reconfigurable fault accommodation rather than isolated coordination design. For survey purposes, they can be viewed as a progression from constraint-aware nominal control ref [45], ref [9] to disturbance-resilient cooperation ref [18], ref [38], and finally to fault-tolerant consensus and formation maintenance under degraded actuation ref [14], ref [37], ref [43], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central safety-critical issue in MAV swarms is fault tolerance under actuator degradation, partial loss of effectiveness, or complete failures. Such faults can rapidly destroy formation geometry, induce inter-agent collision risk, and invalidate nominal consensus assumptions. Distributed fault-tolerant designs therefore augment cooperative controllers with adaptive compensation, fault estimation, or reconfiguration mechanisms so that stability and coordination objectives can be preserved despite local actuation anomalies. This direction is reflected in fault-tolerant time-varying formation control for high-order agents with actuator failures, observer-based adaptive containment under faulty dynamics, and adaptive fault-tolerant control laws for nonlinear multi-agent systems with actuator faults ref [100], ref [101], ref [31].

For swarm operation in realistic environments, fault tolerance must also coexist with hard input and output limitations. This is particularly relevant for MAVs, whose thrust margins are narrow and whose sensing or safety envelopes impose state/output restrictions. Methods that explicitly combine fault handling with constrained control include game-theoretic designs for strict-feedback systems with input saturation and output constraints, prescribed-performance consensus under unknown dead-zone inputs, and guaranteed-cost fault-tolerant control under time-varying actuator faults ref [13], ref [23], ref [38]. Collectively, these works move beyond asymptotic coordination alone toward performance guarantees under degraded hardware conditions.

Another closely related challenge is maintaining collective behavior under exogenous disturbances and uncertain control effectiveness. Disturbance-observer-based containment strategies and leader-following consensus methods addressing unknown control directions and external disturbances are especially relevant, since MAV swarms must remain coordinated under wind, modeling mismatch, and propulsion asymmetries ref [28], ref [22]. Taken together, these studies suggest that resilient MAV swarming requires an integrated treatment of faults, disturbances, and saturation, rather than viewing them as separable design add-ons ref [100], ref [31], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central safety-critical issue in MAV swarms is fault tolerance under tight actuation limits and uncertain dynamics. At the platform level, actuator degradation, dead zones, and partial failures can rapidly destroy formation coherence or trigger cascading collisions if not detected and accommodated online. Distributed fault-tolerant flocking and consensus designs therefore combine local adaptation with disturbance rejection so that cohesion is preserved despite unknown dynamics and exogenous perturbations, as shown in biologically inspired flocking control, observer-based leader-following consensus, and adaptive neural compensation schemes for actuator failures and dead zones ref [107], ref [27], ref [56].

Beyond maintaining agreement, recent work addresses explicit physical constraints together with fault accommodation. Containment controllers have been developed for velocity and acceleration saturations, showing that safe collective motion must respect bounded translational capability rather than relying on idealized inputs ref [12]. Related command-filter-based containment methods explicitly handle actuator failures while avoiding the complexity explosion of repeated differentiation in nonlinear designs ref [21]. For constrained nonlinear agents, distributed consensus laws have also incorporated unknown control directions and position constraints, which is particularly relevant for MAV teams operating in cluttered airspace where both control authority and admissible states are limited ref [43].

A second line of work focuses on timely fault diagnosis and safety-preserving reconfiguration. Event-triggered schemes for simultaneous fault detection and tracking control reduce communication and computation while still reacting to anomalies before performance degradation becomes unsafe ref [41]. In parallel, formation control under obstacle avoidance and switching interaction topologies highlights that resilience must be coupled with motion-level safety guarantees, not treated as a purely regulation problem ref [46]. Collectively, these studies suggest that robust MAV swarming requires integrated architectures in which fault estimation, constrained control, and collision-aware coordination are co-designed rather than layered independently ref [107], ref [12], ref [21], ref [41], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Physical Constraints, Uncertainty, and Safety-Critical Challenges - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final safety-critical dimension in MAV swarms is resilience to actuator faults, partial loss of effectiveness, and degraded control channels. In practice, such failures can propagate through tightly coupled formation or consensus laws, so fault tolerance must be embedded in the distributed controller rather than treated as a supervisory add-on. Adaptive leader-following and consensus designs explicitly compensate for uncertain nonlinear dynamics and actuator malfunctions by estimating fault effects online and redistributing control effort across neighbors, thereby preserving formation coherence under local failures ref [14], ref [41]. Related reconfigurable synchronization strategies for heterogeneous Euler–Lagrange networks further show how constrained coordination laws can maintain bounded cooperative behavior after component degradation, which is directly relevant to heterogeneous MAV teams with unequal payload, propulsion, or sensing capabilities ref [9].

Beyond classical adaptive compensation, several works connect resilience with constrained-input operation. Anti-windup consensus tracking under saturation is important because a damaged MAV often reaches control limits earlier than healthy agents; distributed anti-windup mechanisms reduce instability caused by integrator buildup and improve graceful performance degradation ref [30]. Similar robustness goals appear in iterative learning approaches for uncertain nonlinear leader–follower systems with input saturation, where repeated task execution is exploited to recover coordination accuracy despite persistent model mismatch and actuation limits ref [32]. More general constrained adaptive control frameworks also address simultaneous state, output, and input restrictions, which is essential when emergency maneuvers must remain inside safe flight envelopes ref [17], ref [45].

Recent resilient optimal-control formulations extend this line by using learning-based adaptation to sustain distributed performance under uncertainty and adverse conditions ref [35]. For MAV swarms, the main implication is that safety-critical control should combine fault diagnosis, control reconfiguration, and hard-constraint awareness in a single distributed architecture, rather than optimizing each aspect separately. Such integration is particularly valuable in cluttered or GPS-denied environments, where disturbances, saturation, and failures may occur simultaneously and where maintaining a conservative but connected collective response is preferable to aggressive nominal performance ref [14], ref [30], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first layer of security in MAV swarming concerns resilience of cooperative regulation and consensus to faults, uncertainties, and corrupted interactions. Robust distributed output-regulation formulations provide an important baseline because they explicitly account for plant uncertainty while preserving coordinated tracking objectives across interconnected agents, thereby offering a natural foundation for safety-critical swarm behaviors under imperfect models and disturbed communication channels ref [10]. Related robust consensus designs for heterogeneous matching uncertainties further strengthen this perspective by showing that coordination laws can remain stable even when individual agent dynamics differ and are imperfectly known, which is highly relevant to MAV teams with nonuniform payloads, wear, or environmental exposure ref [18].

Beyond nominal robustness, the literature increasingly treats internal faults as a security-relevant failure mode because actuator or sensor anomalies may be accidental or induced by adversaries. Distributed adaptive fault-tolerant output-regulation and consensus schemes demonstrate that cooperative objectives can be maintained despite uncertain agent dynamics and local failures, often without centralized diagnosis infrastructure ref [17], ref [47]. Complementing reconfiguration-based control, simultaneous fault-detection and consensus design embeds residual generation into the coordination loop, enabling earlier identification and isolation of compromised or malfunctioning units before errors propagate through the swarm network ref [33].

A more explicitly adversarial line of work addresses malicious manipulation of information exchange. Secure impulsive synchronization under deception attacks studies how intermittent corrective actions can counter falsified data injections ref [20], while consensus-tracking methods under multiple attack types examine coordinated performance degradation caused by compromised channels or agents ref [23]. Denial-of-service resilience is also central for MAV swarms because jamming and packet suppression can abruptly fragment the information graph; distributed consensus controllers designed for DoS environments therefore offer a useful template for maintaining bounded degradation and recovering coordinated motion once communication resumes ref [26]. Collectively, these studies frame resilient MAV swarming as a joint problem of robust regulation, fault accommodation, attack detection, and communication-aware recovery.

subsections.section_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central line of work in secure MAV swarming considers resilient consensus under communication-layer attacks and stochastic malicious disruptions. In this context, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks are especially damaging because they intermittently break the information flow required for coordination; distributed secure average-consensus schemes explicitly address this threat by preserving convergence despite attack-induced packet losses and communication blackout intervals ref [25]. Complementary observer-based secure consensus formulations treat random attacks as exogenous disturbances or switching anomalies, using distributed state estimation to recover admissible coordination signals and maintain closed-loop stability ref [44]. For discrete-time networked swarms, attack analysis has further clarified how deception, data corruption, or compromised agents can destabilize nominal update laws, motivating resilient controller redesign at the protocol level ref [35].

Beyond cyber attacks, resilience in MAV swarms must also cover component-level degradation, particularly actuator failures that propagate into formation drift or loss of tracking. Adaptive fault-tolerant consensus-tracking methods compensate for time-varying actuator faults through online parameter adjustment, allowing agents to preserve cooperative objectives without centralized diagnosis ref [43]. Related neural-network-based adaptive designs extend this idea to uncertain nonlinear dynamics and unmodeled fault effects, improving tracking robustness when failure signatures are difficult to parametrize a priori ref [14]. At the formation layer, distributed fault-tolerant time-varying formation control has shown that second-order agents with directed interactions can sustain prescribed geometric patterns even under actuator failures, which is directly relevant to practical MAV team reconfiguration ref [37].

A broader robustness perspective links security-aware coordination with disturbance attenuation and topology-dependent reliability. Distributed reliable H∞ consensus under switching networks provides a useful framework for bounding the impact of exogenous perturbations and topology changes, offering performance guarantees that are attractive for contested or degraded aerial communication environments ref [11]. More generally, anti-disturbance cooperative control highlights how disturbance observers, rejection mechanisms, and compensation loops can be integrated with distributed protocols to enhance swarm resilience against both environmental uncertainty and adversarial manipulation ref [38]. Taken together, these studies suggest that secure MAV swarming is best approached as a joint problem of attack tolerance, fault accommodation, and disturbance rejection rather than as a purely cryptographic or networking issue ref [25], ref [35], ref [44].

subsections.section_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central line of work for secure MAV swarming is resilience at the control layer, where coordination must remain stable despite compromised links, corrupted synchronization signals, or degraded actuators. Resilient synchronization under attacks has been studied explicitly in distributed multi-agent settings, showing how attack-aware protocols can preserve collective timing and state alignment rather than merely detecting anomalies ref [129]. Complementarily, resilient consensus designs for nonlinear agents account for switching topologies and randomly varying communication delays, which is particularly relevant to aerial swarms operating over intermittently connected wireless channels ref [15]. In discrete-time settings, H∞ consensus formulations further address network imperfections and exogenous disturbances, providing a disturbance-attenuation perspective that is directly applicable to adversarial perturbations and packet-level uncertainty ref [34].

Another major theme is fault-tolerant coordination, since actuator degradation and partial control loss can be operationally indistinguishable from malicious interference in MAV platforms. Time-varying formation control with actuator failures has been developed for high-order linear multi-agent systems, enabling geometry preservation despite local loss of effectiveness ref [131]. Related adaptive fault-tolerant schemes for nonlinear agents explicitly compensate actuator faults through distributed adaptation ref [31], while guaranteed-cost formulations quantify the performance penalty incurred under time-varying actuator faults ref [38]. These results are important for swarms because resilient operation is not only about maintaining stability, but also about bounding mission-level degradation during attack or failure episodes.

Containment-oriented resilient control is also highly relevant in leader-follower MAV missions such as convoying, perimeter protection, and cooperative surveillance. Observer-based distributed adaptive fault-tolerant containment control addresses general linear dynamics when direct state information is incomplete ref [132], whereas robust H∞ containment formulations extend this idea to uncertain nonlinear agents and disturbance-rich environments ref [56]. Taken together, these works suggest that adversarial robustness in MAV swarms is best viewed as a layered property combining attack-resilient synchronization, fault-tolerant formation maintenance, and robust containment under uncertainty, rather than as an isolated cybersecurity add-on ref [129], ref [131], ref [132], ref [15], ref [31], ref [34], ref [38], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central line of work in secure MAV swarming emphasizes fault-tolerant consensus and containment under actuator, sensing, and communication anomalies. Rather than assuming perfect agent health, these methods explicitly model failures or malicious perturbations as part of the closed-loop design. Distributed fault-estimation observers enable leader-following consensus despite actuator faults by reconstructing fault signals online and compensating them locally, improving recoverability without centralized supervision ref [27]. Related containment strategies for nonlinear agents with actuator failures use command filters to avoid excessive differentiation while preserving bounded distributed implementation, which is attractive for resource-limited aerial platforms ref [21].

Beyond explicit fault estimation, robustness is also pursued through disturbance attenuation and uncertainty-adaptive control. Distributed output-regulation formulations provide a principled way to maintain cooperative objectives in the presence of exogenous disturbances and model mismatch ref [9], while distributed H∞ consensus under switching topologies strengthens attenuation guarantees when inter-MAV links vary over time ref [31]. For stronger nonlinear uncertainty, adaptive neural approaches compensate unknown actuator failures and dead zones ref [56], and biologically inspired flocking laws incorporate fault tolerance and disturbance rejection directly into distributed motion coordination ref [30]. These approaches are particularly relevant to MAV swarms operating in cluttered or contested environments, where uncertainty and adversarial effects are tightly coupled.

A further trend is the integration of detection and mitigation within communication-efficient architectures. Event-triggered schemes that jointly perform fault detection and tracking control reduce update burden while still isolating abnormal behavior in multi-agent networks ref [41]. At the attack-aware end of the spectrum, non-fragile output-feedback consensus under uniform quantization and deception attacks explicitly addresses compromised information channels, showing how robustness margins can be preserved despite quantized measurements and falsified data streams ref [136]. Collectively, these studies suggest that resilient MAV swarms require not only robust controllers, but also embedded diagnosis, attack-aware filtering, and graceful performance degradation under partial compromise.

subsections.section_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Security, Resilience, and Adversarial Robustness in MAV Swarming - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final line of work particularly relevant to MAV swarms emphasizes resilient performance under simultaneous uncertainty, faults, and maliciously induced disturbances. Rather than treating security as a purely cryptographic layer, these approaches embed robustness into the control law itself through guaranteed attenuation, adaptation, or reconfiguration. Finite-horizon H∞ consensus formulations explicitly address stochastic parameter variations and disturbance rejection over mission-relevant time windows, which is valuable for short-duration but safety-critical swarm maneuvers such as ingress, tracking, or coordinated avoidance under uncertainty ref [21].

Fault-tolerant formation and consensus studies further show how distributed estimation and adaptation can preserve collective objectives after actuator or subsystem degradation. In leader-following settings, adaptive fault-tolerant formation control compensates for nonlinear uncertainty while maintaining cohesion around a designated trajectory ref [14]. Related fault-tolerant consensus designs for fuzzy multi-agent models are important when MAV dynamics or attack effects are represented through rule-based approximations, since they offer a structured way to bound uncertainty and sustain agreement despite component-level failures ref [41].

More recent resilient adaptive optimal control methods incorporate reinforcement learning to recover near-optimal coordination policies online in the presence of adverse conditions ref [35]. For MAV swarms, this suggests a promising direction beyond static resilience margins: agents can adapt their cooperative behavior as attack patterns or fault signatures evolve. However, these methods also highlight an open challenge for aerial swarms: balancing learning-based adaptation with certifiable stability, fast fault isolation, and the stringent computation and communication limits of embedded flight hardware ref [14], ref [21], ref [35], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Representative MAV-swarm applications are most naturally expressed as distributed formation and coordinated navigation problems, where teams must maintain safe inter-agent spacing while traversing cluttered environments. In this context, distributed model predictive formulations are especially relevant because they explicitly encode collision and obstacle avoidance together with formation objectives, making them well aligned with inspection, search, and cooperative transport scenarios in constrained spaces ref [30]. Closely related optimal formation methods under switching interaction graphs further illustrate how application requirements translate into coupled motion-planning and control constraints rather than pure consensus objectives ref [130].

Practical deployments also expose a second application-layer requirement: preserving communication connectivity while respecting limited actuation. For aerial collectives, temporary link loss can quickly degrade localization, coordination, and task allocation; thus bounded distributed controllers that maintain graph connectivity are directly relevant to field operations such as exploration and perimeter monitoring ref [29]. The same concern appears in communication-aware motion planning frameworks, where task specifications must be satisfied jointly with network maintenance constraints ref [72], and in quadcopter-oriented leader-follower coordination studies that account for packet dropouts during cooperative flight ref [89].

Looking forward, application-driven research is increasingly moving toward tighter integration of planning, adaptation, and learning. Distributed learning and cooperative control provide a pathway for MAV swarms to improve coordination policies online under environmental uncertainty ref [25], while consensus-based cooperative learning with neural approximators suggests how data-driven adaptation can be embedded in decentralized architectures ref [56]. Learning-based consensus for heterogeneous nonlinear agents with constraints further indicates the potential for transferring such ideas to more diverse aerial teams ref [103]. A key future direction is therefore communication-control-learning co-design, where safety, connectivity, and task performance are optimized simultaneously rather than handled in separate layers ref [30], ref [29], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental MAV swarms increasingly rely on distributed cooperative-control architectures that can be implemented with limited onboard computation and sparse communication. In this context, general distributed coordination frameworks provide the algorithmic basis for consensus, leader–follower regulation, and cooperative task execution, and remain central to translating multi-agent theory into deployable aerial teams ref [10], ref [92]. For formation-oriented missions, adaptive leader-guided designs are especially relevant because they capture the practical need to track moving targets or dynamically updated waypoints while preserving inter-vehicle coordination ref [27].

A persistent challenge on real platforms is that swarm performance is often constrained less by nominal control design than by safety-critical network effects. Connectivity-preserving control is therefore essential for MAV teams operating in cluttered or GPS-denied spaces, where loss of neighbor links can rapidly degrade localization, consensus, and collision avoidance performance ref [34]. Likewise, disturbance rejection remains a practical requirement for flight in wind, downwash, and modeling uncertainty, motivating distributed anti-disturbance methods that improve collective robustness under environmental perturbations ref [38].

Future research directions point toward secure, learning-enabled, and application-aware swarm autonomy. Security is becoming particularly important as MAV collectives are exposed to packet manipulation, spoofing, and denial scenarios; resilient and observer-based secure consensus designs provide a foundation for maintaining coordinated behavior under such attacks ref [35], ref [44]. At the same time, distributed learning methods demonstrated in neighboring cyber-physical domains, such as multi-agent Q-learning for traffic coordination, suggest a path toward adaptive aerial swarm resource allocation and airspace management policies ref [22]. A key open problem is to unify learning, resilience, and connectivity maintenance within experimentally validated MAV platforms rather than treating them as separate control layers ref [22], ref [34], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A salient future direction for MAV swarms is communication-control co-design, where motion generation, task logic, and wireless constraints are optimized jointly rather than treated as separate layers. This is particularly important in dense aerial collectives, where packet loss, limited bandwidth, and spatially varying connectivity directly affect safety and task completion. Communication-aware planning under temporal and spatial logic specifications provides one promising route, enabling teams to satisfy mission constraints while explicitly accounting for information exchange requirements ref [24]. Related distributed model predictive control formulations further show how consensus and coordinated motion can be maintained for nonlinear second-order agents under dynamic coupling and constraints, which is highly relevant to quadrotor swarm operation ref [32].

Another key trend is the reduction of communication and computation load through event-triggered and self-triggered coordination. Instead of periodic broadcasting, agents update only when local conditions justify it, improving scalability and onboard efficiency for resource-limited MAVs. General event-triggered control strategies establish this principle at the network level ref [45], while self-triggered methods reduce continuous monitoring requirements and are attractive for embedded aerial platforms with strict energy budgets ref [49]. More specialized event-triggered formation stabilization and tracking results also suggest practical mechanisms for maintaining geometric patterns in cooperative flight with fewer transmissions ref [52].

From an application perspective, these ideas support long-endurance surveillance, infrastructure inspection, and adaptive environmental monitoring, where aerial teams must reconfigure around obstacles and changing communication topology. Distributed optimal control with obstacle avoidance is therefore directly relevant to safe deployment in cluttered spaces ref [51]. More broadly, swarm-intelligence perspectives continue to motivate decentralized adaptation and robustness at scale ref [49], while cross-domain multi-agent applications such as distributed microgrid management highlight useful design principles for large heterogeneous networks, including resilience, locality, and hierarchical coordination that future autonomous aerial collectives may increasingly adopt ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central future direction for MAV swarms is the co-design of communication, formation control, and platform architecture. Practical deployments must tolerate packet loss, asynchronous updates, and topology changes while preserving collective objectives. This is evident in leader–follower quadcopter coordination under packet dropouts, where communication unreliability directly affects tracking and stability margins ref [40]. Related distributed formation methods further show that obstacle avoidance and switching interaction graphs cannot be treated as secondary add-ons, but must be embedded into the control layer from the outset ref [46].

At the algorithmic level, resource-aware coordination is increasingly important for onboard implementation. Asynchronous event-triggered circle formation illustrates how communication can be reduced without requiring strict synchronization, which is attractive for low-power MAV teams with heterogeneous sensing and computation budgets ref [51]. Likewise, distributed adaptive distance-based formation and flocking control highlights the value of local geometric constraints that scale naturally with team size and can accommodate modeling uncertainty ref [53]. Together, these works point toward swarm controllers that are sparse in communication, adaptive in behavior, and robust to non-ideal network conditions ref [40], ref [51], ref [53].

These control advances also motivate new experimental platforms. Hardware perspectives from swarm robotics emphasize reconfigurability, self-reassembly, and modular system design, suggesting longer-term convergence between MAV swarms and physically reconfigurable robotic collectives ref [45]. For aerial systems, this implies that future testbeds should not only validate formation and flocking laws, but also expose interactions among vehicle design, communication stack, and distributed autonomy. Bridging such hardware–algorithm gaps remains a key challenge for realizing large-scale autonomous aerial collectives in cluttered, dynamic environments ref [45], ref [46], ref [53].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Applications, Experimental Platforms, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major future direction for MAV swarming is the transition from controlled demonstrations to mission-oriented, heterogeneous, and learning-enabled aerial collectives. Experience from competition-driven benchmarking shows that realistic rescue scenarios expose integration gaps between perception, autonomy, and team coordination that are often hidden in simplified laboratory tests, motivating more rigorous evaluation protocols for robustness and scalability ref [44]. Application-oriented studies such as swarm-based mine detection further illustrate that coverage efficiency alone is insufficient; practical deployment also depends on uncertainty handling, false-alarm management, and coordination under sparse sensing ref [49]. More broadly, algorithmic analyses of collective systems emphasize that the coupling structure among agents and environment strongly shapes what forms of swarm intelligence are computationally and physically realizable, a point highly relevant to resource-constrained MAV networks ref [36].

Progress on experimental platforms is similarly pushing the field toward modularity and heterogeneity. Modular swarm testbeds such as Groundscouts demonstrate the value of reconfigurable hardware/software stacks for rapidly prototyping cooperative behaviors and evaluating distributed coordination principles under repeatable conditions ref [38]. At the system level, heterogeneous swarm integration has highlighted the importance of middleware, interoperability, and task-level orchestration when aerial vehicles must cooperate with ground or virtual agents ref [55]. Early distributed robotics platforms and collections of experimental results reported in distributed autonomous robotic systems research also remain instructive, particularly in showing how platform design choices constrain attainable collective behaviors and reproducibility ref [56]. Hybrid physical-virtual experimentation, as explored in predator-pursuit domains, further suggests a practical route for scaling learning and adaptation before full real-world deployment ref [53].

Looking ahead, learning-based adaptation is likely to become increasingly central, but only if coupled with safety and resilience guarantees. Reinforcement-learning-based resilient adaptive optimal control offers one template for embedding online performance improvement into distributed systems subject to disturbances and uncertainties ref [35]. For MAV swarms, however, the key open problem is not merely adding learning, but co-designing communication, control, and experimentation pipelines so that adaptive policies remain verifiable, transferable across platforms, and robust in heterogeneous multi-robot missions. Competition-inspired benchmarking, modular platforms, and mixed-reality training environments together provide a plausible pathway toward larger autonomous aerial collectives operating in complex public-safety and inspection applications ref [44], ref [38], ref [53].
